tags.name: FS
tags.description:
FS exposes a read-write file system over RPC with the rpc surface of
[types.WriteFS]: the read surface of [types.ReadFS] — metadata lookup,
directory listing, symbolic link resolution and streaming file content — plus
whole-file upload, directory creation and deletion, and one metadata read
covering the file system itself. It is the service a server implements for a
file system that answers to [types.WriteFS], so its rpcs cover each distinct
method reachable from that interface exactly once, and none of them asks for a
capability that [types.WriteFS] does not promise.

The interfaces reachable from WriteFS overlap heavily: [types.WriteFS] is
[types.ReadFS] plus [types.RemoveFS], [types.RemoveAllFS], [types.CreateFileFS]
and [types.MkdirAllFS]; [types.ReadFS] is [types.SimpleFS] plus the four
extended read interfaces of the standard library, [fmt.Stringer],
[types.DeviceInfoGet], [types.URIGet] and [types.ComparableFS]; and
[types.RemoveFS], [types.RemoveAllFS], [types.CreateFileFS] and
[types.MkdirAllFS] each embed [types.SimpleFS] of their own. A method several
interfaces carry is therefore exposed once rather than once per interface,
which is why there is one GetFile rather than one for [fs.StatFS] and one for
[types.ReadFS].

Each rpc maps one-to-one onto a Go method: the rpc name is the method name,
the request message carries that method's arguments, the first argument is
bound into the URL and the rest travel in the request body. The verbs
(":readLink", ":mkdirAll", ":removeAll") mirror the Go names instead of
following an AIP-133 resource model, so the rpc-to-method mapping stays
auditable line by line; designing collection-shaped URLs is a separate
decision from this file. A method whose Go signature returns only an error
returns [google.protobuf.Empty].

The rule bends in one place, deliberately: [GetMetadata] answers three Go
methods in one rpc. Each of the three is still answered exactly once, but in
one round trip rather than three, which is what separates a method call from a
network call. [types.URIGet.URI], [fmt.Stringer.String] and
[types.DeviceInfoGet.DeviceInfo] are three cheap calls in Go that say the same
thing about a file system whichever path they are asked about, so they are
answered by one [FileSystemInfo] that a client reads once and caches. An
answer that changes from path to path is not folded in, because caching it
once would make it wrong for the next path.
[types.CreateFileFS.Create] is the other way round: it takes nothing but a
name and returns a live [types.File] handle, which is not a value that can
cross the wire, and what a client wants after it is the content in the file —
so it has no rpc of its own and is answered by [WriteFile], which creates the
file and carries its content in one request rather than two.

Errors follow the standard gRPC canonical codes: a path the file
system does not hold returns NOT_FOUND (wrapping fs.ErrNotExist), a path
that already exists where the call needs it not to returns ALREADY_EXISTS
(wrapping fs.ErrExist), an operation the backend refuses returns
PERMISSION_DENIED (wrapping fs.ErrPermission), and a path that
[fs.ValidPath] rejects returns INVALID_ARGUMENT (wrapping fs.ErrInvalid).

Two Go methods reachable from [types.WriteFS] are deliberately not rpcs.

[io.Closer.Close] is left out because it tears down the entire underlying
file system rather than acting on a single request, and a server cannot decide
when every client it serves is done with a file system it was handed.

[types.ComparableFS.IsSame] asks whether two file systems hold one set of
data. All a client can name on the wire is a location, and ComparableFS
states that it answers a different question from the one that compares
locations: an "other uri" argument would implement location comparison under
the name IsSame and report the wrong answer for a cache or a mount point.
What a client can compare instead is the uri field of [GetMetadata].

What [types.WriteFS] does not reach has no rpc either. [types.OpenFileFS],
[types.RenameFS], [types.MkdirFS], [types.CopyFileFS], [types.LinkFS],
[types.ChmodFS], [types.ChownFS], [types.LchownFS], [types.ChtimesFS],
[types.BatchCreateFS], [types.Watcher], [types.ClosestParentFS],
[types.MountedArchiveDirFS], [types.ReleaseFS], [types.WrapperFS] and
[types.ExternalPathGetFS] are interfaces a file system may or may not carry,
so an rpc for each of them would make the surface a server offers depend on
the file system standing behind it, and a request for something that file
system cannot do would have to be refused or answered with an emulation the
file system never promised. The same reasoning keeps [types.WrapperFS.InnerFS]
out: it hands back an [fs.FS] value rather than data.
[types.ExternalPathGetFS.ExternalPath] is kept out for a further reason: a
client already has that address, since it reaches the file system through a
grpc:// address that names the server and the path inside it, and constructs
that address itself rather than asking for it.

Three of the cuts need a word, because a read and a write of the same thing
fall on different sides of the line. Reading a symbolic link is
[fs.ReadLinkFS.ReadLink], which [types.ReadFS] carries, so [ReadLink] stays
while creating one does not. A node's mode and timestamps are answers
[fs.StatFS.Stat] gives, so [File] still reports them even though changing
them has no rpc. [types.MkdirAllFS.MkdirAll] is part of [types.WriteFS]
whereas [types.MkdirFS.Mkdir] is not, so a client that wants a directory
creates the chain.

get.summary:
GetMetadata is the single metadata read about the file system itself: one
rpc answering what three Go methods report, in one [FileSystemInfo].
get.description:
Its uri, description and devices fields answer [types.URIGet.URI],
[fmt.Stringer.String] — which [types.ReadFS] and [types.StringerFS] both
carry — and [types.DeviceInfoGet.DeviceInfo]. None of the three is about a
path, which is why the request names none: one answer describes the whole
file system.

One rpc rather than three because a method call in Go and a round trip are
not the same price: the answer is meant to be read once and cached by the
client, which is also why there is no field selector for asking a subset of
it. A file system that does not implement one of those interfaces leaves the
fields it would have filled at their zero values, and an error status is the
failure of the read as a whole.

get.summary:
ListFiles returns the immediate children of a directory. Equivalent to
[types.ReadFS.ReadDir], which is [fs.ReadDirFS.ReadDir].

parameters.name: parent
parameters.description:
The directory whose immediate children should be listed. "." lists the
root directory.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description:
The maximum number of files to return. The service may return fewer
than this value. If unspecified, the server picks a reasonable default.

parameters.name: pageToken
parameters.description:
A page token received from a previous ListFiles call, used to retrieve
the next page.

post.summary:
WriteFile writes a whole file in one call, as [types.WriteFileFS.WriteFile]
does: the file is created if necessary and truncated first, and the
parents are not created. It is also how [types.CreateFileFS.Create] is
answered — see the service comment — so creating a file and filling it is
one request, and a reader never sees the empty file that creating it and
then writing it would expose.
post.description:
A single small upload is the common case. The 10 MB ceiling above which a
file is worth streaming rather than sending whole is a server policy, not
part of the wire format, so it is recorded here rather than as a field a
client could set: below it a client puts the content in one frame — one
HTTP request body — and above it the content arrives in the stream this rpc
is.

The upload is a client stream so that a file larger than the server will
accept in one message still fits, and so that grpc-gateway can proxy the
call from an ordinary HTTP request body. The whole file is still one
request, which is what WriteFile is: no partial write and no seek.

The URL names no path parameter, because a client-streaming rpc cannot
carry one: the path of the file travels in the first frame, so the HTTP
form is a POST whose whole body is the file.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description:
WriteFileRequest is one frame of a [WriteFile] upload. name and mode are
read from the first frame and ignored in the rest, which is what lets
grpc-gateway proxy the call from one HTTP request body; data chunks arrive
in order and are concatenated into the file's whole content. An empty stream
writes an empty file. (streaming inputs)

get.summary:
GetFile returns metadata for the node at name. Equivalent to
[types.ReadFS.Stat], or [types.ReadFS.Lstat] when symlink_handling is
SYMLINK_HANDLING_NO_FOLLOW.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path of the file to retrieve.

parameters.name: symlinkHandling
parameters.description:
Whether to follow a trailing symbolic link at name. Defaults to
SYMLINK_HANDLING_FOLLOW.

 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_UNSPECIFIED: Equivalent to SYMLINK_HANDLING_FOLLOW.
 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_FOLLOW: Follow the symbolic link and describe its target. Equivalent to
[types.ReadFS.Stat] / [fs.Stat].
 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_NO_FOLLOW: Do not follow the symbolic link; describe the link itself. Equivalent to
[fs.ReadLinkFS.Lstat].

delete.summary:
Remove deletes the file or empty directory at name, as
[types.RemoveFS.Remove] does. A non-empty directory is an error; so is
removing the root.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path of the file or empty directory to delete.

post.summary:
MkdirAll creates the directory at name and any missing parents, as
[types.MkdirAllFS.MkdirAll] does. It is a no-op if the directory exists.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path of the directory to create, together with any missing parents.

get.summary:
ReadFile streams the content of the file at name. Equivalent to
[types.ReadFS.ReadFile], or to [fs.FS.Open] followed by reading what the
handle gives. [fs.FS.Open] returns a handle rather than data, so this rpc
is how a reader reaches it; what a handle does once it is open — a position
that moves, a partial write, a seek — has no rpc here.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path of the file to read.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description:
The byte offset to start reading from. 0 reads from the start of the
file.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description:
The maximum number of bytes to return across the whole stream. 0 (the
default) reads to the end of the file.

get.summary:
ReadLink returns the destination of the symbolic link at name. Equivalent
to [types.ReadFS.ReadLink], which is [fs.ReadLinkFS.ReadLink].

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path of the symbolic link to resolve.

delete.summary:
RemoveAll deletes name and everything below it, as
[types.RemoveAllFS.RemoveAll] does. A name that does not exist succeeds.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The path to delete, together with everything below it.

mode.description:
Permission bits for newly created nodes, as defined by Go's
io/fs.FileMode.

name.description:
The name of the device, as given by the operating system or by the ufs
implementation. "default" when the backing device is not known.

deviceType.description:
The kind of device behind a path (e.g. "disk", "tmpfs", or an
object-storage scheme). "unknown" when it cannot be reported.

threadCount.description:
The recommended number of concurrent accesses for the device; 1 is the
answer for a device that should not be walked in parallel.

ufsDeviceInfo.description:
DeviceInfo describes one backing device of a file system, mirroring
[types.DeviceInfo]. It is platform-agnostic on purpose: a client need not
know how the server's operating system names devices in order to decide how
hard to drive it.

The remote flag that [types.DeviceInfo] carries is deliberately not on the
wire. A file system reports remoteness to itself, for the process that holds
it; to a client of this service everything is already remote, so the field
would answer the same question for every device and answer it before the
client has made a single call. How much a device is worth driving is what
device_type and thread_count are for.

name.description: The path of the file, relative to the root of the file system.

size.description: Length in bytes for regular files; system-dependent for others.

mode.description: File mode bits, as defined by Go's io/fs.FileMode.

modTime.description: The time the file was last modified.

isDir.description: Whether the file is a directory. Equivalent to mode's directory bit.

ufsFile.description:
File is the resource representation of a node (regular file or directory)
in a [types.ReadFS] tree. It mirrors [types.FileInfo].

File names follow [fs.ValidPath]: forward-slash separated, no leading
slash, no "." or ".." components. The root directory is always ".".

uri.description:
The URI that identifies this file system, as [types.URIGet.URI] reports it,
the method [types.URIGetFS] carries as well. Can be passed to ufs.New to
reconstruct an equivalent file system. Empty if the file system has no
meaningful URI.

description.description:
A human-readable description of how the file system is composed, as
[fmt.Stringer.String] reports it — the method that [types.ReadFS] and
[types.StringerFS] both carry. Intended for debugging and logging, not
programmatic use.

devices.description:
Which device backs which path, as [types.DeviceInfoGet.DeviceInfo] reports
it, the method [types.DeviceInfoGetFS] carries as well: the [types.DeviceMap]
keyed by path, with "." for the root. The map is minimal, naming a path only
where the backing device changes, and a path with no entry of its own is
backed by the entry of its nearest ancestor, which is the lookup
[types.DeviceMap.Backing] performs. The map covers the whole file system in
one answer, which is why it is here rather than being asked per path.

ufsFileSystemInfo.description:
FileSystemInfo is the metadata a file system reports about itself: what the
file system is, not what one path inside it is. [GetMetadata] is the only rpc
that returns it and returns every field in one answer: these facets are
separate Go methods but one network read each, so the rpc answers all of them
at once and a client reads this message once and caches it instead of paying a
round trip per facet. A file system that does not implement the Go interface
behind a field leaves that field at its zero value.

It is still the singleton resource of AIP-156 that it was: there is exactly
one per file system, it has no name field, and no field below changes from
path to path. What a file system answers per path does not belong here,
because a client wants those where it is working on the path rather than once
for the file system.

files.description:
The immediate children of the requested parent directory, sorted by
filename, as returned by [types.ReadFS.ReadDir].

nextPageToken.description:
A token that can be sent as page_token to retrieve the next page. Empty
if there are no more files.

data.description:
A chunk of file content. Chunks are delivered in order starting at
offset and are concatenated by the client to reconstruct the requested
range.

target.description:
The destination path of the symbolic link, as returned by
[types.ReadFS.ReadLink]. May be relative to the link's directory.

ufsSymlinkHandling.description:
SymlinkHandling controls whether a lookup follows a symbolic link to its
target or reports on the link itself.

 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_UNSPECIFIED: Equivalent to SYMLINK_HANDLING_FOLLOW.
 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_FOLLOW: Follow the symbolic link and describe its target. Equivalent to
[types.ReadFS.Stat] / [fs.Stat].
 - SYMLINK_HANDLING_NO_FOLLOW: Do not follow the symbolic link; describe the link itself. Equivalent to
[fs.ReadLinkFS.Lstat].

name.description: The path of the file to write.

mode.description:
Permission bits for a file that is created, as defined by Go's
io/fs.FileMode. A file that already exists keeps the permissions it has.

data.description: Part of the file's content, in order.

ufsWriteFileRequest.description:
WriteFileRequest is one frame of a [WriteFile] upload. name and mode are
read from the first frame and ignored in the rest, which is what lets
grpc-gateway proxy the call from one HTTP request body; data chunks arrive
in order and are concatenated into the file's whole content. An empty stream
writes an empty file.
